sections.body_en:
The difference between the two prohibitions, theft (geneiva) and robbery (gezela), is that the thief is one who comes secretly and, without the owner's knowledge, steals property or money, whereas the robber is one who snatches an object or money from the owner's hand by force. Of course, both the thief and the robber must return what they took or pay the value of what they took. But the difference between them is that the robber always pays only what he robbed, whereas the thief, the one who comes at night and in secret, if witnesses testified against him before an ordained beit din [that is, one whose judges received semikha from the Sages, one from the mouth of another, back to Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him], must pay double what he stole. And today, when there is no Sanhedrin and no ordained beit din, the beit din has no power to judge laws of fines, and the thief too pays only the value of what was stolen.

And another important law to know: by Torah law a person is forbidden to steal money or objects from his fellow, even if their value does not reach a peruta. That is, the matter does not depend on the value of what is stolen; rather, every theft, however trifling it may be, is forbidden by Torah law. And one must further add that not only stealing an object permanently is considered theft, but also one who steals in order to return it, who wants to use his fellow's object for a certain time and afterwards return it – this act too is considered theft.

To sum up, the Torah prohibition of stealing or robbing in practice includes all the objects of another person, and anyone who uses them without permission, even for a short time, transgresses the prohibition of theft.

And there are some who sometimes play tricks on their friends, and without their knowledge take some important object from them, and afterwards enjoy watching them worry and search nervously for the object that has disappeared. It is clear that one who does this transgresses a Torah prohibition, by the very fact that he causes his fellow distress. But regarding the prohibition of theft, the commentators disagreed about the level of severity of theft done as a game. Some say that theft in a game too is forbidden by Torah law. And some say that since the matter is done as a game, and not in order to use the friend's object, there is therefore no Torah prohibition of theft in it, but the Sages forbade doing so, so that people would not become accustomed through such a game to steal in earnest. But as stated, even if from the aspect of the prohibition of theft there is only a rabbinic prohibition here, nevertheless by the very causing of distress to the friend, one transgresses a Torah prohibition (Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, Laws of Theft and Robbery 1-3).

sections.title_en: 2. Robbing and Stealing from a Gentile
sections.body_en:
It is forbidden to steal or rob from a gentile even something of trifling value (Bava Kamma 113b). And likewise it is forbidden to mislead the gentile – for example, to confuse him in the reckoning so that he thinks he must pay the Jew more than he needs to. And likewise if the Jew bought something from the gentile on credit, and the gentile forgot that the Jew owes him money, the Jew is obligated to pay him.

And if the gentile erred of his own accord – for example, he owes the Jew a sum of money for several things, and the gentile calculated his debt and erred and thought he had to pay more – the Jew is not obligated to correct him and tell him that he must pay less; rather, he may say to him, "I am relying on your calculation," and take the money. And if the Jew wants to sanctify the Name and tell the gentile that he erred and receive less money, this is praiseworthy. And when there is concern that a ḥillul Hashem may be caused – that perhaps it will become clear to the gentile that he erred and he will resent the Jew for not correcting him – in such a situation the Jew is obligated to make the gentile aware of his error and to receive the payment due to him and no more (SA ḤM 348:2).

And there is a tradition in Israel that those who profited from the errors of gentiles did not see blessing in their toil, and their property went to ruin and they left no blessing after them. Whereas those who sanctified the Name and returned money of gentiles that had reached them by mistake grew and became wealthy and prospered, and left their abundance to their children (Sefer Ḥasidim 661).

The prohibition of theft applies also to things of trifling value. One may not take any object of one's fellow without permission, even if its value is very small, less than a peruta. For example, one may not enter a neighbour's house and take from there even a small teaspoon without permission. And even in order to return it, it is forbidden, because one who borrows without the owner's knowledge, that is, without the owner's permission, is considered a thief.

Nevertheless, there are exceptions to this law, and with cheap things that it is the way of the world not to be particular about at all, a person is permitted to use another person's objects without explicit permission. For example, a person passing along the road who needs a small splinter to pick his teeth with is permitted to take a small splinter from a private person's fence; and likewise when a person needs a match, and the owner of the box of matches is not present, it is permitted to take one match. And the same law applies to using a friend's simple and cheap pen, which one may use even without explicit permission.

But this permission is subject to two conditions. The first, that the owner of the object not be in the area, so that it is not possible to ask him for permission. For if it is possible to ask permission, one must do so, and make sure that he indeed agrees. And the second condition, that it is the way of the world to take these objects without permission, and that that person – the owner of the box of matches, for example – is not known as particular and stingy, and therefore presumably he agrees that people use his trifling objects.

And although by law one may be lenient, it is a trait of piety to be stringent when possible, and not to use anything of one's fellow, not even a pen or a match, without explicit permission (Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, Theft 1; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan ḤM 359:1).

sections.title_en: 4. One Who Borrows Without the Owner's Knowledge
sections.body_en:
One of the questions that arise from time to time is: is a person permitted to use his fellow's object without his permission? For example, it happens that a person wants to hoe his garden a little, but his hoe has been lost, and his neighbour is not at home; and the question is, may he take his neighbour's hoe without asking permission? Or another example: two friends who live together in a dormitory, and one of them has a radio – may the roommate use his friend's device without explicit permission? And since questions of this kind arise very often, it is very important to clarify this question in principle.

First, we have already mentioned that even theft in order to return is considered theft; if so, it is clear that taking an object without the owner's consent is considered theft and is forbidden by Torah law. But the question is what the law will be in the case of good friends, when one of them is not present and his friend wants to use one of his objects. It is very likely that the owner of the object is willing for his friend to use it without his permission; the question is whether one can in practice rely on this likelihood.

Let us narrow the question somewhat. It is clear that if there is even one percent chance that the friend will resent that his object was taken without permission, then certainly, according to all views, in such a case it is forbidden to borrow an object from him without permission; for the prohibition of theft is a Torah prohibition, and as long as there is a doubt one must be stringent.

The poskim disagreed about the question of what the law will be when it is one hundred percent clear to a person that his friend agrees that he use his objects even without his permission – whether in such a case it is permitted to use them or not. In the view of the Gaon Rabbi Zalman of Liadi (Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, Laws of Found Property 1), even though he is one hundred percent sure that his friend agrees, as long as he has not received explicit permission he is forbidden to use the object without permission. But in the view of the Shakh (ḤM 358:1), since it is entirely clear that the owner of the object agrees, and he has no possibility of asking his permission, it is permitted to use it without explicit permission. And in practice the custom is to be lenient in accordance with the view of the Shakh, and it is a custom of piety to be stringent when possible.

Similar to the previous halakha, it sometimes happens that a person who was at a wedding or another public event goes to take the suit jacket he had left on the hanger, and to his surprise it becomes clear to him that the jacket has disappeared, and in its place there is another jacket, rather similar. And the question is what to do – may he meanwhile take that jacket or not?

The Shulḥan Arukh ruled in Ḥoshen Mishpat (136:2): "If his garments were switched in the house of mourning or in the house of a feast, he shall not use them." And this is because a person is forbidden to use another's objects without permission. And although one can surmise that a mix-up happened here, and that the jacket that remained belongs to the same person who took his jacket by mistake, so that in practice they are exchanging their jackets, and each one is using his fellow's in place of his own, nevertheless this is not certain, since it is possible that the jacket was taken by mistake by some third person, or was stolen; and therefore he is forbidden to take the jacket that remained.

And likewise the reverse: a person who was confused and took by mistake a jacket that is not his, and when he returned to take his own jacket he found no jacket in the place, is forbidden to use the jacket he took by mistake; its law is like the law of a lost object he found, which he is forbidden to use, and he must announce that he found a jacket, and likewise announce that he lost another jacket.

And if the owner of the jacket that is with him comes to take it, how good; and if not, after a time passes in which it is reasonable that the owner of the jacket has given up hope of it, he should note down for himself its price, and he may use the jacket; and if the one who lost it comes, he shall return its monetary value to him. And the same law applies to bags that were switched and anything similar (Milei de-Nezikin, based on the proposal of Rabbi Moshe Feinstein, responsum 9).

But there are garments which, in the case of such a mix-up, it has become customary to use, like a raincoat or an umbrella: if they were switched by mistake, the way of the world is that in the meantime each one uses his fellow's. Indeed, in the view of the Gra"z of Liadi, even in such a case it is forbidden to use one's fellow's without permission. Nevertheless, the custom is to rely on the one who is lenient. And the principle is that the custom is to be lenient in things that people generally are not particular about, and where, on the other hand, if they are not used in the meantime, distress will be caused to both, as for example with coats or umbrellas, for if they are not used in the meantime they will not be able to go out in the rain.

And as stated, even in this there are those who follow a custom of piety, and in no way use another's objects without asking explicit permission (those who are lenient are the Shakh 358:1 and Arukh Ha-Shulḥan ḤM 136, and so I heard in the name of Rabbi Shlomo Zalman Auerbach, and so wrote Rav Batzri in Dinei Mamonot; and in the Shulḥan Arukh of the Gra"z he was stringent).

A question that arises from time to time: is a person who took part in a wedding permitted to take a little of the food for his wife or his children?

One must divide the question into two parts. There is food that remains on the individual plate, and there is food that remains in the communal serving bowls.

As for the food that remains on a person's individual plate, it is certainly about to be thrown away, and since nobody will derive any benefit from it, it is permitted to take it home. And all this on condition that the matter is done in a polite manner that will not detract from the honour of the hosts of the celebration.

And the food that remains in the communal bowls generally belongs to the hosts of the celebration, or to the owner of the hall, or to the catering company, and everything depends on what they agreed among themselves. When the food left in the communal bowls belongs to the hosts, they are permitted to take it to their home or to return it to the owner of the hall in exchange for a reduction in payment. And in these cases it is clear that one who wants to take from what remains in the communal bowls or in the bottles must ask permission of the hosts.

And if the guest claims, "But I received a family invitation for my wife and children, and since they did not come I am permitted to take their portion home," we will answer him that the food was bought only for those who came to gladden the groom and bride, and not for whoever received the invitation; and since they did not come to gladden, they have no permission to take the food home. And our Sages already said in tractate Berakhot (6b) that anyone who benefits from a groom's feast and does not gladden him transgresses against the five voices with which the Torah was given.

And in cases where what remains belongs to the owner of the hall, the guest is forbidden to take of the food left in the communal bowls. Only if it is known that in any case everything that remains is going to be thrown away, and the wedding has already ended, is the guest permitted to take of what remains even without permission (see Responsa Shevet Ha-Levi 4:225).

Although we hold as a general principle that one may not take any object belonging to someone else without explicit permission, and one who takes it transgresses the prohibition of theft, nevertheless regarding objects of a mitzva, such as a tallit or tefillin, the law is different. The reason for this is that since it is known that a person is interested in taking part in the doing of a mitzva, and there is also no concern that damage will be caused to the tallit or the tefillin, the matter is therefore considered as though there were a fixed and general permission here covering everyone, that a person agrees that his mitzva objects be used even without his permission. And the same law applies to the four species, a shofar and the like. And so it was ruled in the Shulḥan Arukh (OḤ 14:4).

But this permission is subject to five conditions. The first, that if the owner of the object is in the area, one must ask him for permission, and only if it is not possible to ask his permission is it permitted to use his mitzva objects without permission. The second condition, that the use of the mitzva object be occasional; but one who wants to use his fellow's tallit regularly is obligated to ask his permission. The third condition, that the borrower use the mitzva objects only in the place where they are lying, and not take them out to another place, so that if his fellow comes he will be able to find his objects immediately; and also because many are particular about this – they indeed agree that their tallit be used, but they do not agree that the borrower treat it like an owner and take it wherever he wishes. The fourth condition, that the borrower return the tefillin or the tallit to their place and put them down exactly as they were, without any change. And the fifth condition, that if it is known that the owner of the tallit or tefillin is a particularly exacting person, and it is possible that he does not agree that even his mitzva objects be used without permission – it is forbidden to take his objects without explicit permission.

And because of the fifth reason, several poskim of the later generations, such as the Ben Ish Ḥai (Year 1, Lekh Lekha 6) and Arukh Ha-Shulḥan (OḤ 14:11), hold that in our times the law has changed, and today one should not wrap oneself in a tallit or put on tefillin of someone else without asking him explicit permission. Their reason is that today habits of cleanliness have changed, and many cannot bear others wrapping themselves in their tallit because of the sweat, especially when the tallit is clean and new.

And in practice, a person who finds himself in a synagogue without a tallit is forbidden to simply take a tallit without permission, especially if it is lying in a hidden place. Only if there are people there who say that it seems reasonable to them that the owner of the tallit would agree to its being worn without permission – only then is it permitted to wrap oneself in it. And when it is not known whether he agrees, it is better to pray without a tallit than to enter into a doubt of robbery. And one who is lenient to wrap himself in a tallit and put on tefillin that are not hidden away has someone to rely on.

But regarding the four species of the festival of Sukkot, for example, there is no concern at all, and a person is pleased that a mitzva be done with his property, and it is permitted to take them without permission under the conditions detailed.

A further question in the laws of one who borrows without the owner's knowledge is whether a person is permitted to read his friend's books without asking permission. Of course, if the owner of the book is present, it is forbidden to take his book without asking permission. The question is what the law is when he is not present.

As for a secular book, it is clear that the book's law is like that of any object, and it is forbidden to take it without explicit permission. And if it is one hundred percent clear that the owner of the book agrees that it be used, we have already learned (in halakha 3) that there is a dispute about this; and according to most poskim in such a case it is permitted to use the book, and some are stringent. And the custom is to be lenient.

And as for a holy book, seemingly the law is more lenient: since we have a principle that a person is pleased that a mitzva be done with his objects, then even when we personally do not have one hundred percent certainty that the owner of the book agrees, one can lean on the principle that a person is pleased that a mitzva be fulfilled with his property, and use his book without permission. But this principle applies only where there is no concern that the object will be damaged, as for example with tefillin; but regarding study in a book there is concern that the book will wear out, and therefore the Rema ruled (OḤ 14:4) that even a holy book may not be used without its owner's permission.

However, all this is said regarding prolonged study in a book; but it still needs to be clarified what the law will be regarding a light glance of a few moments, or, for example, borrowing a siddur for one prayer only. In the view of the Mishna Berura, since it has already been ruled that it is forbidden to use a friend's book without permission, there is no distinction between prolonged study and a light glance, and in any case one may not take a book without permission (MB 14:16, based on the Peri Megadim). But in the view of Arukh Ha-Shulḥan (14:13), a person is permitted to glance lightly in his friend's book or to pray from his siddur even without permission, and the custom in our times is to be lenient in accordance with the view of Arukh Ha-Shulḥan.

And it may be that a further reason to be lenient is joined here: for the source of the law that it is forbidden to borrow holy books without permission was stated regarding books that were written by hand, and their price was very high, and any slight damage would cause great distress to the owner of the book; and therefore it was clear that even though there is a mitzva in study, a person does not agree that his books be touched without permission. But today, when the price of books is relatively cheap, presumably a person is pleased that a mitzva be done with his books, even though they may get somewhat creased. And therefore the custom today is to be lenient, and when it is not possible to ask permission of the owner of the book, it is permitted to glance in it lightly, and likewise it is permitted to pray from his siddur. And some are stringent and do not take even a holy book without explicit permission.

It is forbidden to take a book out of the library of a synagogue or beit midrash without the permission of the gabba'im or the librarians, even though the book is intended for the use of the public. And although seemingly a person could claim that by taking it home he will be able to study more in the book, and thereby add to the mitzva of Torah study, nevertheless since the book belongs to the public, and there are gabba'im appointed on behalf of the public over the library, one is necessarily obligated to ask their permission in order to take the books and use them.

And even if in that synagogue where the books are kept there is nobody who studies in them, it is forbidden to take them without permission. For since they belong to the public, one who takes them without the gabba'im's consent takes them by theft.

But on the other side, there is an obligation on the gabba'im of the synagogue to lend books to whoever needs to study in them. For there is a halakha (SA ḤM 163:1) that the people of a town compel one another to take part in buying books of the Torah, Prophets and Writings, so that each of the townspeople can study in them. And the Sma wrote about this that today, when books are readily available, the townspeople cannot compel one another to buy them, because nobody has a problem obtaining a Tanakh. But it is clear that there is a mitzva to establish in every synagogue a public library in which there will be many books that a private person cannot afford to buy. And if some person wants to study a certain book at his home, the gabba'im are obligated to lend him the book; and if they do not agree to lend it, the beit din must obligate them to lend it, because of bittul Torah (Sma there, based on the Rema 292:20; Igrot Moshe ḤM 1:39).

And when there are many learners who use the books, and it is possible that at the same time that this person takes the book home, other people will need it in the library, in such a case the gabba'im are entitled not to lend out any book, so that anyone who wants to study in the books should come to the synagogue library and study.

sections.title_en: 10. Stealing to Be Saved from Death by Starvation
sections.body_en:
An interesting question in the laws of theft is whether a poor person who has nothing to eat is permitted to steal in order to save himself from death by starvation. It is completely clear that according to halakha, if that poor person has the possibility of asking help and charity from his acquaintances, or even from strangers, he is certainly forbidden to steal, and he must turn and ask their help. There is no shame at all in this; on the contrary, it is his sacred duty to turn for help in such a situation.

And although the Shulḥan Arukh wrote (YD 255:1): A person should always keep himself far from receiving charity, and bear hardship, so that he will not need other people. And so the Sages commanded: Make your Shabbat like a weekday, and do not need other people. And even if he was an honoured sage and became poor, he should engage in a craft, even a lowly craft, and not need other people. Nevertheless, the Shulḥan Arukh wrote further on that anyone who needs to take charity and cannot live unless he receives charity – such as an old person, or a sick person, or one who is suffering – and he is proud and does not take it, so as not to need other people, he is a shedder of blood and forfeits his life. And he has no benefit from his suffering, but on the contrary, iniquities and sins. And this is because a person bears an obligation to take care of his own survival, and if he cannot earn a living and sustain himself by his own strength, he is obligated to ask for help.

But in a case where all the doors of the generous have been shut, and nobody is willing to help, and the person reaches a situation where, if he does not immediately steal food to keep himself alive, he will die of hunger – in such a case it has been ruled in halakha that it is permitted to steal. And not only this, but in the book Yam Shel Shlomo it is written that not only is he permitted to steal, but he is obligated to steal in order to save his life from death; and if he did not steal and died, he forfeits his life. But a condition must be added here: that even in such a case it is forbidden to steal except with the intention that after a time, when the thief's situation improves, he will pay the price of what was stolen to its owners.

And so the Shulḥan Arukh ruled (ḤM 359:4): "Even if he is in danger of death and needs to rob his fellow in order to save his life, he must not take it except with the intention of paying" (Bava Kamma 60b, Tosafot, Rosh and Yam Shel Shlomo; Tur and SA ḤM 359:4).

sections.title_en: 11. Taking Another's Property to Save One's Own
sections.body_en:
It is indeed a well-known halakha that a person is forbidden to use his fellow's property without permission, and one who uses it without permission is a robber. But there is a situation in which it will be permitted to use another's property even without receiving permission. And this is when a person suffers sudden damage that could not have been foreseen. For example: a person walking on the road holding a jug full of honey, and suddenly his jug breaks and the honey begins to spill, and he sees before him an empty jug that belongs to another person. The halakha is that he is permitted to take the jug without permission and immediately pour the honey into it, and thereby save it.

The root of the halakha lies in the enactments of Yehoshua bin Nun: at the time the Children of Israel entered the Land, Yehoshua stipulated several conditions in monetary law. And one of them is that if a person suddenly suffers great damage, he may make use of another's property in order to save his own money. The reason for the enactment is that if, in situations of sudden damage, we had to search for the owner of the vessel in order to ask his permission, time would pass and we would no longer be able to prevent the damage. Therefore Yehoshua enacted that if the owner of the vessel is in the area, he is obligated to extend help immediately, and if he is not present, a person is permitted to take his objects and use them in order to save his own property. Of course, if the vessels he took without permission are damaged, he will have to pay for the damage.

And the same law applies in a case where a person learned of great damage that happened suddenly in his factory, and he must reach the factory within a few minutes in order to repair the fault and save his property, and his car is not available to him – he is permitted to take his friend's car without permission, and of course with full responsibility for any damage that happens to the car.

But there is a case in which the poskim disagreed whether a person is permitted to save himself with another's property without permission. And this is when the other's property will be lost entirely. To explain the halakha, let us return to the previous case, where a person is walking with a jug full of honey, and suddenly the jug breaks and the honey begins to spill. But instead of finding an empty jug, he finds a jug full of wine, and the price of the wine is lower than the price of the honey. In the view of several poskim, among them Arukh Ha-Shulḥan (ḤM 264:14; 308:14), he is permitted to pour his fellow's wine onto the ground and put the honey in its place, and afterwards pay his fellow the full price of the wine, and the honey will remain his. But in the view of the Gra"z (Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, Laws of Borrowing 6), it is fitting for a conscientious person to be stringent, because in such a case he is not only using his fellow's property without permission but even destroying it entirely; and only if he knows that his fellow will not mind is he permitted to pour out his wine and put the honey in its place.

sections.title_en: 12. One Who Sees That His Fellow Is Being Robbed
sections.body_en:
It sometimes happens that a person enters a shop, and suddenly he notices that one of the customers is stealing something from the shop. The question is what he must do. Is he obligated to help the shopkeeper prevent the theft, or is he permitted to evade the matter and act as one who saw nothing? It should be noted that a person is generally afraid to intervene in such cases, and the question is whether, because of fear or discomfort, he is permitted to evade helping his fellow.

In the midrash of the Sages in the Sifra (on Vayikra 19:16) they said: From where do we know that if you know testimony in favour of your fellow you are obligated to go and testify, and you are not permitted to keep silent? The verse teaches: "You shall not stand by the blood of your fellow." And so the Rambam ruled (Sefer Ha-Mitzvot, negative commandment 297) that included in the mitzva "You shall not stand by the blood of your fellow" is also the obligation to save your fellow's money. That is, we are obligated to save not only his life but also his property. If so, it is clear that a person who sees that his fellow is being robbed, or that his property is being damaged, must do everything in his power to prevent the theft (Aseh Lekha Rav 6:85, 100).

However, ideally it is best to do this in a way that will not cause great humiliation to the thief, for it is possible that that thief is not accustomed to this, and perhaps one small remark will be enough for him to stop his theft. Therefore, one should first whisper in his ear that he should not steal. And if even then he does not stop, one should shout at him in a loud voice, so that the other people will hear and come to the shopkeeper's aid. And the same law applies to a person who sneaks onto a bus without paying: one should tell him gently that he needs to pay. And if he is not persuaded immediately, one must tell the driver. For there is no difference between stealing from a private person and stealing from a public body like Egged or Dan (and in the book Dinei Mamonot vol. 4, p. 6, he wrote otherwise).

And if the person fears for his life – that if he comments, perhaps they will harm him – in such a case he is not obligated to intervene immediately, but he must be ready to complain to the police and afterwards testify against the thief. But together with this, one should not be so afraid; on the contrary, if thieves know that the public as a whole fights against them, they will certainly decrease, and great good will grow from this for the people of Israel.

sections.title_en: 13. Putting an Employee to a Test of Theft
sections.body_en:
A question that people sometimes wrestle with is whether a person is permitted to test his employee, in order to check whether he is an honest person. For example, is it permitted to say to the employee, "Buy me something in the shop with these fifty shekels, and return the change to me," while at the same time putting a hundred shekels in his hand? And to wait for the change and see whether the employee will exploit the employer's supposed mistake and do the reckoning as though he had received only fifty shekels, or whether he will admit the truth and tell his employer, "You made a mistake and gave me more money than you thought."

The same question is asked also regarding a cleaning help – whether it is permitted to put her to a test. For example, that the lady of the house leave a sum of money in a place visible to the help, and afterwards go out and leave the help alone in the house, in order to check whether she will lay her hand on the money.

In the book Dinei Mamonot by Rav Batzri (vol. 4, p. 10) he ruled, based on Responsa Torah Lishmah (siman 407), that a person is forbidden to put his fellow to a test, lest the fellow indeed be tempted and sin; and it turns out that the one who tested him transgressed the prohibition "And before a blind person you shall not put a stumbling block" (Vayikra 19:14).

But in Responsa Aseh Lekha Rav (vol. 7, 71, 100) he brought the view of the Yaskil Avdi (vol. 7, 44:17), who ruled that an employer is permitted to put his workers to a test in order to check their level of trustworthiness.

And it seems that in practice it is permitted to put the employee to a test, on condition that the test is not different from, or harder than, the tests the employee will face in the course of his work. As, for example, a cleaning help to whom the house is about to be entrusted: it is certain that throughout her work she will face a constant test; if so, placing the sum of money before her is not a special stumbling block. For if she wants to steal, she will be able to do so easily in the course of her work, only then the lady of the house will not know about it, for a person does not check every day whether all his objects are in their place. Whereas through the test the lady of the house can learn clearly and immediately about the character of the help. And on the contrary, it is possible that precisely if the help fails the test, in the end she will steal less; and there is no prohibition here of "And before a blind person you shall not put a stumbling block."

And the same law applies to every worker and employee: his employer is permitted to test him with all those tests which in any case he will have to face in the course of his work.

But to put the help or the employee to harder tests than those they will have to pass in the course of their ordinary work – about this there is a dispute: some forbid it because of the prohibition "before a blind person you shall not put a stumbling block," and some permit it since there is benefit in it of preventing thefts.

A person who works in an office or in a factory too must beware of the prohibition of theft at his place of work, for there are prohibitions that many people are not aware of. For example, a clerk is forbidden to use the telephone without the employer's explicit permission. And likewise, a place that allows its employees to make only cheap calls (for example, within the same telephone network) – no employee may violate this and make expensive calls; and even if that employee does not use his right to make cheap calls, and only rarely needs expensive calls, he may not make expensive calls without explicit permission from the employer (Aseh Lekha Rav 5:102).

And even when the office agrees to cheap calls, it certainly does not agree that the employee make a great many calls; therefore, in any case where it seems to the employee that perhaps he is exceeding the permission that was given, he must ask special permission for that excess. And the same law applies to using the office's paper and envelopes: the employee is forbidden to use them for his private needs without explicit permission.

And it is important to pay attention to a further point. Sometimes the work manager does not have the authority to give permission to make phone calls or to use office property for private needs, because he is not the owner; but since he is the senior person, the employees ask him for permission to call and they call, and it is possible that in practice both of them become partners in theft. Therefore, when the employee asks the work manager for permission, he must make thoroughly sure that he indeed has the right to give permission.

And Rav Yehuda already said (Bava Batra 165a) that most people stumble in robbery. And Rashi explained that the meaning is not that most people actually intend to steal, but because money is dear to a person, while his fellow's money is not so important to him, therefore many people rule leniently for themselves and are not careful enough with other people's money, and unwittingly stumble in robbery.

sections.title_en: 15. Cursed Is One Who Misleads a Blind Person on the Way
sections.body_en:
We were commanded (Vayikra 19:14): "Before a blind person you shall not put a stumbling block, and you shall fear your God; I am the Lord." And likewise it is said (Devarim 27:18): "Cursed is one who misleads a blind person on the way." In addition to the simple prohibition of not tripping up a blind person and not directing him onto crooked paths, our Sages explained that anyone who is not versed in a certain field is considered blind in that field, and one who misleads him transgresses a Torah prohibition.

For example, a seller of electrical appliances who understands and is expert in the quality of electrical products, and knows that an electrical product of a certain company tends to break down quickly: if, when a customer asks him for advice about buying that product, he praises the product and conceals the defects known to him, he transgresses a Torah prohibition. And likewise one who works in insurance or banking, and a client comes to him to ask his advice, and he gives him a misleading answer that will cause him not to be able to receive the best terms – about him it is said: "Cursed is one who misleads a blind person on the way."

The Torah used the example of a blind person because every person understands that tripping up a blind person on his way is a wicked act; and in exactly the same way one must know that one who trips up his fellow with bad advice, which will cause him loss or much trouble, is like one who trips up a blind person on his way.

And if the one who gave the misleading advice also profits from it – for example, the seller of electrical appliances receives additional percentages of profit from that company so that he will promote its products – then in addition to putting a stumbling block, he has also defrauded and robbed him of his money. And likewise, if that bank employee or insurance agent profits from having given the client bad advice, he transgresses also the prohibition of ona'ah (fraud). And although there is no way to prove that the one who tripped up his fellow intended to do so, nevertheless before the Holy One, blessed be He, these things are known, and He will call his iniquity to account; and this is what is said (Vayikra 19:14): "Before a blind person you shall not put a stumbling block, and you shall fear your God; I am the Lord."

Just as a person is forbidden to rob his fellow's money, so an employee is forbidden to idle from his work. As the Shulḥan Arukh wrote (ḤM 337:20): "The worker is warned not to idle a little here and a little there, but he must be exacting with himself about time."

And one must be so careful not to steal the employer's time that the Sages said that workers doing work for an employer shorten Birkat Ha-Mazon: they say the first blessing as instituted, and in the second they open and close with the blessing of the Land and include in it "Who builds Jerusalem", and the fourth blessing – "Who is good and does good" – they do not say at all; for since it was the Sages who instituted saying it, they cancelled their enactment so as not to steal the employer's time. Indeed, already from the period of the Rishonim all employers have been accustomed not to be particular about this, and consequently the obligation returns to the workers to say the whole of Birkat Ha-Mazon (SA OḤ 191:1-2).

Another halakha that teaches us how careful the worker must be not to steal the employer's time: although the Sages enacted that three who ate together are obligated in zimmun, if they are workers and one of them finished his meal before his fellows, he should bless without zimmun so as not to be delayed from his work. Only if the employer agreed that they wait for one another for zimmun may he delay until the zimmun (MB 191:2).

We learned the foundation of this from Yaakov Avinu, about whom the Torah takes the trouble to tell us again and again of his great devotion to his work, as he said to Raḥel and Leah (Bereshit 31:6): "And you know that with all my strength I served your father." And likewise he said to Lavan, who pursued him (Bereshit 31:39-40): "That which was torn by beasts I did not bring to you; I bore the loss of it; of my hand you required it… Thus I was: by day the heat consumed me, and the frost by night, and my sleep fled from my eyes."

Yaakov Avinu also attributed his rescue to the merit of his devoted work, as our Sages said (Bereshit Rabba 74:12): "Labour is more beloved than the merit of the fathers, for the merit of the fathers saved money, and labour saved lives." As it is said (Bereshit 31:42): "Had not the God of my father, the God of Avraham and the Fear of Yitzḥak, been with me, surely now you would have sent me away empty-handed; God has seen my affliction and the labour of my hands (that is, my devoted work), and He rebuked you last night" (and prevented Lavan from killing me and my sons).

Therefore the worker should not lose heart, and should not think, "What value is there in my toil?" For the work of one who does it faithfully is great in the eyes of the Holy One, blessed be He. And diligence and faithfulness in work is the tested remedy for wealth (see SA ḤM 337:20; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan ḤM 331:3).

And the employee must sleep and eat properly, for if he is tired or hungry he turns out to be robbing his employer (SA ḤM 337:19).

And if the employer and the employee agreed on the working hours and the circumstances in which the employee may stop his work – their agreement decides. And if they did not agree – the custom of the place decides. But it is very hard to determine what the custom is. For it is clear that in the most urgent cases it is customary to speak on the telephone; the question is what is defined as urgent. And likewise it is permitted to make a cup of tea; the question is how much time is lost around preparing the tea and drinking it. To get out of the doubt, it is good to agree on these matters explicitly with the employer.

sections.title_en: 17. Some Laws of Ona'ah in Buying and Selling
sections.body_en:
"And if you sell something to your fellow or buy from the hand of your fellow, do not wrong one another" (Vayikra 25:14).

Ideally, sellers and buyers must not wrong one another, and must sell and buy everything at the accepted price in that place and at that time (even if there are small gaps).

And if they erred and carried out the sale at a difference of more than a sixth from the accepted price – for example, an object whose accepted price is about six hundred shekels was sold for seven hundred and one shekels – the buyer can cancel the sale. And likewise if that object was sold for four hundred and ninety-nine shekels, the seller can cancel the sale. And if before the sale the seller told the buyer, "I know that such an object can be bought for only five hundred, but I want seven hundred for it," and the buyer agreed to pay seven hundred, he cannot afterwards retract and claim that the seller defrauded him, since he informed him in advance that he was charging him more than the accepted price. When is there a claim of ona'ah? When the matter was done unknowingly.

And if the error was to the extent of a sixth of the accepted price, there is no possibility of cancelling the sale, but the one who wronged his fellow must return the sixth by which he wronged him. (A sixth means the range between a sixth from within, 14.2%, and a sixth from without, 16.6% – Sma 227:3.)

And if they erred by less than a sixth of the value of the sale, the sale stands, and the side that profited need not return what he profited, since it is less than a sixth, and the way of the world is to forgo such an error, because it is hard for the buyer and the seller to fix the price of the sale precisely (SA ḤM 227:1-4).

It should be noted that in modern commerce there are enormous gaps between the prices of many products according to the type of commerce: a wholesaler is not like a retailer, and a sale by tender or on the internet is not like a sale in a shop. Therefore our words refer to buying in an ordinary shop; but in other types of commerce there is sometimes no accepted price at all, and consequently the law of ona'ah changes.

And all this applies specifically when the error was in fixing the price, that they estimated the value of the goods as more or less than its worth. But if it was agreed that the goods cost a hundred shekels, and they erred in counting the banknotes, and the buyer paid more or less, then even if the error was of one shekel, the sale stands and the shekel must be returned (SA ḤM 232:1; Sma 2).
